bio.en: Marc Benioff is the founder, chairman, and CEO of Salesforce, the cloud CRM pioneer he started in 1999 that grew into one of the world's largest enterprise software companies.
bio.zh: 马克·贝尼奥夫（Marc Benioff）是 Salesforce 的创始人、董事长兼 CEO，这家云 CRM 先驱公司始于 1999 年，已成长为全球最大的企业软件公司之一。

summary.en: Marc shares his philosophy of compassionate, stakeholder-centered capitalism and how Salesforce pioneered cloud software and the "1-1-1" philanthropy model. He discusses leading through massive scale, the role of trust as the #1 value, and how to keep innovating as a large company. The episode is a rare look at building and running an enduring tech institution.
summary.zh: 马克分享了他"以人为本、兼顾各方利益相关者"的资本主义理念，以及 Salesforce 如何开创云软件与"1-1-1"慈善模式。他探讨了在巨大规模下如何领导、为何把"信任"作为第一价值观，以及大公司如何持续创新。本期罕见地展示了如何构建并运营一家经久不衰的科技机构。

turns.en: I keep having these existential freakout moments about AI. This is really moving fast.

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: It's a great story, but it's really a story about my relationship with Steve Jobs. When I was in college in 1984, I had the opportunity to be an intern at Apple. I wrote the first native assembly language on the Macintosh. It's a crazy thing to be able to say, but it's true that I was writing these example programs for this Macintosh 68000 Development System on these Apple headquarter buildings in Bandley, Bandley Road in Cupertino and started to have a relationship with Steve Jobs in that... Not that I was actually talking to him. I was like this snot-nosed 19-year-old kid, but he's running around the building. We have this refrigerator over here with all these fruit juices. There's a masseuse over here doing shots and massages. There's a motorcycle in the lobby. There's a pirate flag on the roof, and there's Steve Jobs running around, yelling at everybody, and it was freaking cool. (07:10): Okay. So you can just imagine like you're like, "Whoa, this is like I'm in a movie." There's a lot of other cool parts of a movie too that were going on, and it started my relationship with him, and then I actually got to know him then as I eventually got to Oracle. Then, eventually, I started Salesforce, and I had this moment at Salesforce. It was, I think, 2000, 2001. I cannot remember exactly what it was, and we were at the opening of one of his movies for Pixar, and we're having dinner. There's a lot of details around the dinner. It'll be a hugely long story if I go forever. (07:56): He says to me, "Well, Marc, now, listen to me. You're doing so great. You've got your company, Salesforce. If you need any help, you make sure you call me, okay?" I'm like, "Yes, sir. I will do that." He took out his... He had just introduced the iPod, and he's like, "I got a thousand songs in my pocket here. Look at this, and that, and all that." It's this cool device. I'm like, "That's such a cool screen. Steve." He goes, "Oh, thanks so much." I go, "Steve, you could do movies on there too, not just... or photos. You didn't have to do songs." "No, Marc. I will never do a device like that. Absolutely not." (08:34): That's a little insight into his personality that he would never ever exactly say, "Oh, yeah, I'm going to do the movie device that have the photo, the phone, the this." So, anyway. Things were moving along at Salesforce, and so I was like, "I'm stuck, and I need to get through my block, writer's block, entrepreneur's block. I'm going to reach out to him." He's like, "Come down here right away." (09:03): So, literally, I got in my car, brought a few of my team with me, and we go down, and he's like, "Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah, you're blocked. There's three things you need to do right now." I'm like, "Okay. What are they?" He go, "Your company, it better get 10 times larger than it is now in 24 months or it's over." "Oh, okay. Yes, sir. Yes, sir." "Number two, you better sign a huge customer for this Salesforce automation product like Avon. They're a great salesforce." The CEO of Avon was on his board at the time, so that was on his mind. "And one last thing I'm going to tell you you must do." I'm like, "Yes, sir. What is it?" "You better go build an application economy." "An application economy?" "Yes." "What does that mean?" "I don't know, but you're going to go figure it out." (09:55): It was like meeting with your guru and getting a Zencon or something where you're... Now, you have a puzzle I have to solve. I literally went away, and I had all the notes from the meeting. I went through it over and over again. Then, finally, I'm like, "I think he wants me to build an app store." At that moment, I went to the domain registry, and I bought appstore.com. Then, I started working on it at Salesforce so that we would have the ability with our platform to build apps, and then sell them, and that you could do all these things. (10:34): So I did all that and launched AppExchange in 2005 or 2006. We didn't call it App Store because when we tested the App Store name in focus groups, customers are like, "This is not an app store. This is an app exchange. We're all going to exchange apps and capabilities with each other." Anyway, it rolled out, iPhone rolled out, and then he basically said to me one day, "Hey, come down and see me." This is maybe a year after iPhone. I'm like, "I'll be right down." (11:08): I get down there, and I have some team members with me. They'd heard this story before, et cetera, and then we're sitting there like this in the Apple Auditorium. It's not like in a hotel or anything. I remember it very clearly like it was yesterday. He said, "I brought you all down here today." It's very good theatrical performance. I could never do what he does. It's incredible. He's got the thing, and then he says, "And I'm here to reveal to you the App Store." All of our people go, "Huh." They're doing break breath, and they're all like... go white because they're like, "Oh, Marc has been talking about App Store for years. How could Steve even..." (11:51): Then, at the end of it... It's all over. Everyone leaves the auditorium. They're all going out to play with the App Store and all these things. I walked down. He's sitting down there by himself working on something. He's in the corner of the stage. I go, "Hey, Steve. Can I talk to you for a second?" He goes, "Of course." Very generous with me. Very kind with me. I go, "Steve, I'm going to give you a gift." "Wow, but Marc, what are you are going to give me?" "Steve, I'm going to give you something you don't have, but maybe you'll need, which is the appstore.com URL, appstore.com, and the trademark for App Store because after that meeting we had six years ago, I ended up trademarking these things and buying this URL." He's like, "Oh, it's very nice, but you know this App Store thing isn't going to be very big. Whatever, but thank you very much." That was the story of App Store. It's amazing. It was a very amazing relationship that I had with him. Very grateful to have that relationship and dramatically influenced me in my career and my whole life.
turns.zh:
这是个很棒的故事，但说实话，它更多关乎我与史蒂夫·乔布斯的关系。1984年我在大学时，曾有机会在苹果公司实习。我编写了Macintosh上的首款原生汇编语言。能说出这些事简直不可思议，但确实，我在库比蒂诺班德利路苹果总部的Macintosh 68000开发系统上，为这些示例程序编写代码，并由此与史蒂夫·乔布斯建立了联系……倒不是说我真的和他说过话。当时我还是个19岁的毛头小子，然而他却在大楼里到处跑。我们那边有个冰箱，里面装满各种果汁。旁边还有按摩师提供按摩服务。大厅里停着摩托车。屋顶上挂着海盗旗，史蒂夫在四处指挥，冲每个人大喊大叫，整个场景酷毙了。（07:10）：好吧，你可以想象自己会惊呼：“哇，这简直像电影里的场景。” 当时还有很多其他令人惊叹的片段。这段经历开启了我与他的缘分。当我最终加入甲骨文后，才真正了解他。后来我创办了Salesforce，在Salesforce的某个活动上，我有过这样一个难忘的时刻。大概是2000或2001年，我记不清具体时间了，我们在皮克斯电影首映式上共进晚餐。晚餐的诸多细节至今历历在目。若是继续细说，那可真是长篇大论了。（07:56）：他对我说：“马克，现在听好了。你做得很棒。你创办了Salesforce公司。如果需要帮助，一定要找我，好吗？” 我回答：“好的，先生。一定。” 他拿出刚推出的iPod，对我说：“我口袋里有1000首歌。看看这个，还有那个，还有所有这些功能。” 这设备太酷了。我说：“这屏幕太棒了，史蒂夫。” 他说：“哦，太感谢了。” 我说：“史蒂夫，你本可以在这上面做电影播放功能的，不只是……照片功能。” 他说：“不行，马克。我绝不会做那种设备。绝对不会。” （08:34）：这让我略窥其性格——他绝不会直言：“哦，对，我要做那种集照片、通话、自动化功能于一体的设备。” 总之，Salesforce的事业蒸蒸日上。我陷入瓶颈，急需突破创作障碍，于是决定向他求助。他说：“立刻来见我。” （09:03）：于是我开车前往，带上几位团队成员。他说：“哦，对。你现在遇到了瓶颈。有三件事你必须立刻做。” 我问：“好的，三件事是什么？” 他回答：“你的公司必须在24个月内扩张到现在的10倍，否则就完了。” 我说：“好的，先生。” 第二件事：“你必须为Salesforce自动化产品签下像雅芳这样的巨头客户。他们可是优秀的销售团队。” 雅芳的CEO当时是他的董事会成员，所以这件事对他很重要。最后一条：“你必须去构建应用经济。” 我问：“应用经济？” 他说：“是的。” 我问：“这是什么意思？” 他说：“我不知道，但你得自己想清楚。” （09:55）：这就像与大师会面后获得启迪，接着你就得去破解难题。我带着会议笔记反复思索，最终领悟他的深意。
建一个应用商店。” 那时，我去域名注册网站，买下了appstore.com。然后，我在Salesforce上着手开发，让我们的平台具备构建应用并销售的能力，让用户能完成这些操作。（10:34）：所以我完成了这些工作，于2005或2006年推出了AppExchange。我们最初没叫它“App Store”，因为在焦点小组测试这个名字时，客户反驳道：“这不是应用商店，而是应用交换平台。我们都是在互相交换应用和功能。”不过产品还是上线了，iPhone也问世了。大约一年后，他突然叫我去见他：“嘿，下来见我一面。”（11:08）：我带了些团队成员过去。他们之前听过这个故事，诸如此类。然后我们坐在苹果礼堂里——不是在酒店之类的地方。我至今记得清清楚楚，就跟昨天一样。他说：“今天我把你们召集到这里。”这表演太出色了。我永远也做不到他那样，真是不可思议。他先是讲了一番，然后说：“现在我要向你们揭晓App Store。”我们所有人都惊呼：“哇？”大家倒吸一口凉气，都目瞪口呆，脸色苍白，心里想：“天哪，马克都念叨App Store好多年了，史蒂夫怎么会……” （11:51）：最后，会议结束了。所有人离开礼堂，跑去体验App Store之类的。我走过去，他独自坐在台边工作。走近时，他说：“嘿，史蒂夫，能聊两句吗？”他回答：“当然可以。”对我非常客气。我说：“史蒂夫，我要送你一份礼物。”“哇，但马克，你要送我什么？”“史蒂夫，我要送你一样你没有但可能需要的东西，就是appstore.com的域名和App Store的商标。毕竟六年前那次会议后，我把这些都注册下来了。” 他说：“哦，真贴心，但你知道这个App Store不会火的。随便啦，不过还是谢谢你了。” 这就是App Store的故事。太神奇了。我和他之间的关系令人惊叹。很感激能有这样的缘分，它极大地影响了我的职业生涯和整个人生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's one thread that I love about everything you shared. Here is how generosity was at the center of so much of this, him helping you, you helping him, just wanting to help each other.
turns.zh: 关于你分享的所有内容，有一点让我深有感触。慷慨始终是其核心——他帮助你，你帮助他，大家都心甘情愿地互相助力。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: He is a very generous person, and I'll tell you that he never turned down anything that I asked him to do. I have so many stories, but one story was I was thinking about buying this house, and I wasn't sure should I buy this house, Should I not buy this house, whatever, and so he went... He said, "I'll go look at it for you." So he went, he is looking at this house, and then he calls me, and he goes, "Well, I don't know if you should do this or that, but this might be good. Maybe it is good. Maybe it is a good idea." (13:41): Then, I'm emailing with him after that, and he's very sick, and it's all very sad. Then, he sends me an email, and the last email he sent to me was he said... I said, "Wow. Well, this has worked out better than I thought." He goes, "Marc, everything has worked out so much better than we could have ever imagined." It was just a beautiful thought and incredibly sad all at the same moment, and that was my last correspondence with him.
turns.zh: 他是个非常慷慨的人。我可以告诉你，他从不拒绝我的任何请求。我有太多故事要讲，但最难忘的是我考虑买房那次。当时我犹豫不决，纠结买还是不买，结果他主动说……“我去帮你看看。”他看完后给我打电话，说：“嗯，我不确定你该不该这么做，但这个房源可能不错，或许值得考虑。”（13:41）之后我和他邮件沟通时，他病得很重，整个过程令人心碎。他最后发来邮件时说：“马克，一切都比我们想象得顺利得多。”那一刻，美好与悲伤交织，这是我和他最后的通信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like we could do Steve Jobs stories all day.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们可以一整天讲乔布斯的故事。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Yeah. Oh, no, I have hours.
turns.zh: 是啊，不不，我能讲好几个小时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, you can.
turns.zh: 当然可以。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: I have a lot of Steve Jobs stories, but-
turns.zh: 我有好多乔布斯的故事，不过——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Yeah. Anyway, those are a couple of them.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过以上就是其中几个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By the way, I also love that he had B2B SaaS advice here like, "You need a big customer. You need to hire ACVs, build the marketplace."
turns.zh: 对了，他还提到B2B SaaS方面的建议，比如“你需要一个大客户。要招募ACV（年度合同价值），搭建市场平台。”

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Oh, he hated those. He hated SaaS, and he hated that I was doing enterprise software.
turns.zh: 哦，他特别讨厌那些东西。他讨厌SaaS，也讨厌我做企业软件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, he did.
turns.zh: 是啊，他确实说过。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: He's trying to talk me out of being an enterprise software executive. He's like, "Now, Marc, what are you going to do? You're going to go home and tell your kids that you're working on enterprise software? Who do you sell to, CIOs? Have you had met them? How can you be doing this? I can't imagine a more horrible career." I'm like, "I love it, Steve." "No, Marc, you cannot love this. This is not great." It was really a funny thing. He really disliked that, but yet, he was incredibly supportive of me. He would call me all the time. It was really amazing, actually.
turns.zh: 他一直试图劝我别做企业软件高管。他说：“马克，你现在打算怎么办？回家跟孩子们说你在做企业软件？你卖给谁？CIO（首席信息官）吗？你见过他们吗？你怎么能做这个？我简直无法想象还有比这更糟糕的职业。”我说：“我喜欢啊。”“不，马克，你不能喜欢这个。这太糟糕了。”那真是件趣事。他明明很反感这行，但又对我特别支持。他老是给我打电话。说真的，这太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It feels like a place he was wrong in the end here, which is cool, cool to know. I want to go in a different direction.
turns.zh: 是啊。这感觉像是他最后错判了形势，不过知道这点挺好的。我现在想走不同的路了。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: He was rarely wrong, by the way, so.
turns.zh: 对了，顺便说一句，他很少出错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He was rarely wrong with B2B SaaS. $350 billion of value. Who would've known it existed? Speaking of that, so I want to zoom back to the beginning of Salesforce and when you launched Salesforce. It's crazy to think back to that when basically, you were trying to convince people the future of software was not desktop software, it was going to be in the cloud, it was SaaS. You had all these end of software logos. You had mascots walking around with this no software thing. You hired fake protesters at... I think it was Siebel's conference. It was very hard.
turns.zh: 在B2B SaaS方面他也很少出错。市场价值3，500亿美元。谁能想到它会存在呢？说到这，我想回溯到Salesforce刚起步的时候，你们推出Salesforce的时候。回想起来真是不可思议，当时你们试图说服人们相信软件的未来不在于桌面软件，而是在云端，即SaaS。你们用了那些“软件已死”的标语，还有吉祥物到处宣传“没有软件的世界”。你们甚至在……我记得是在Siebel的会议上雇了假抗议者。那真是太难了。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: I think you read one of my books, Lenny.
turns.zh: 我觉得你读过我的一本书，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know the history of a lot of these things.
turns.zh: 我对很多这类事件的历史都比较了解。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Oh, okay.
turns.zh: 哦，好吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's one of the most legendary launch events in startup history, so I've heard of it many times at this point.
turns.zh: 这是创业史上最具传奇色彩的发布会之一，所以我听过很多次这个故事。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: It was a crazy moment. I mean, Siebel, who was really the enterprise software company doing CRM, was doing a user conference. I was looking for an opportunity to launch our product, so we hired a bunch of actors. They were doing this event in San Francisco, and San Francisco is very woke, so people expect a good protest. So we got some picket signs at Home Depot and made some signs that said, "The end of software is near," and all kinds of other... "No software," and all these things. We had a lot of funny things on signs. We were running a protest outside of Siebel that they were in the software business, but we were like, "Oh, no, we've got to get out of software. We've got to create the end of software." So we have picketers outside of the streets. (16:50): Anyway, he comes out himself out of the building and really gets super upset. Right then, we hit a button, and we have other actors in a van who come out, and they are staging themselves as news crew. So they are like KNMS, K No More Software, and we're like... They're interviewing the protesters. So now he thinks that it's a media thing. He calls the police. He got very upset. He's a great guy. By the way, I love Tom Siebel. I think he's also one of the great entrepreneurs of our generation. He's just fuming, and he doesn't know what's going on. He doesn't exactly know it's us, and we're just having the best time. That night, we had our huge launch event at one of the top theaters in San Francisco. We hired a great band, and it was really... We just had so much fun. It was just a really great time. That was all happened. I remember very well. It was February 22nd of 2001 or 2000, 2000, February 22nd, 2000.
turns.zh: 那真是个疯狂的时刻。我是说，Siebel——当时是一家做CRM的企业软件公司——正在举办用户大会。我当时想找个机会推出我们的产品，所以我们雇了些演员。他们在旧金山举办活动，而旧金山又是个很关注社会议题的地方，所以人们期待会有大规模抗议活动。我们从家得宝买了些抗议标语牌，还制作了写着“软件时代即将结束”的标语牌，以及其他诸如“不许用软件”之类的标语。我们的标语牌上写了很多搞笑的内容。我们在Siebel大楼外举行抗议活动，他们可是做软件业务的，但我们却大喊：“哦，不，我们必须摆脱软件行业。我们要终结软件时代！”于是我们在街边安排了抗议者。（16:50）反正，他亲自从大楼里出来，变得非常生气。就在那时，我们按下按钮，车里的其他演员假扮成新闻摄制组人员，模仿KNMS（K No More Software，意为“软件已死”）的新闻采访。我们采访抗议者。而他以为这是一场媒体行动，还报了警。他非常生气，但完全不知道这是我们搞的把戏。顺便说一句，我很喜欢汤姆·西贝尔。我认为他也是我们这一代最伟大的企业家之一。他气得发狂，却又不明白发生了什么。他根本不知道这是我们干的，而我们却乐在其中。那天晚上，我们在旧金山顶级剧院举办了盛大的发布会。我们请了一支很棒的乐队，整个场面真是……我们玩得非常开心。那真是段难忘的经历。我记得很清楚。是2001年2月22日还是2000年2月22日？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. I haven't heard that interview, the reporter part of that story before.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个故事。我之前从未听过那次采访和记者部分的内容。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: It was crazy.
turns.zh: 太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it, and it sounds frivolous potentially, but I think the genius of this that I want to touch on is-
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个故事，尽管听起来可能有些轻率，但我认为其中的智慧之处——

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: "Frivolous" is a good word. It probably was frivolous.
turns.zh: “轻率”这个词用得恰如其分。当时确实挺轻率的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I imagine is you're trying to get people to even know Salesforce exists, to differentiate, to get the name out, and I feel like that's something a lot of founders struggle with. They don't really know how to get their name out, how to get people to pay attention. Just looking back at that success, I guess, just any lessons from what you did right to get the word "Salesforce" out to get people to pay attention at all to what you were doing?
turns.zh: 所以我猜你们当时是想让人们知道Salesforce的存在，树立品牌形象，扩大知名度。我觉得这是很多创始人都面临的难题。他们不知道如何推广品牌，让人们关注到他们。回顾这场成功，我想问问您，从推广Salesforce这个品牌，让人们注意到你们的业务这方面，有什么成功经验可以分享吗？

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Well, it's a noisy world, Lenny, and you can see that. You can get on Twitter. It's like... I mean, there's a lot of noise, and how do you break through? We have that challenge today. We're introducing a huge new product called Agentforce. I've only been working on it for a couple months now. I introduced it at our Dreamforce Conference, and that was one way to break through, which was I took our conference and said, "It's just going to be about Agentforce." I'm trying to think about, "What are all the things I need to do to get my company 100% on Agentforce, my customers, everyone?" because I know I have a window of opportunity here. (19:25): We're first, we're ahead. We have hundreds of customers on this now. We're on it, which is amazing. We've moved our whole help infrastructure to Agentforce. We're seeing incredible results. We've cut our human escalation from our support infrastructure down by 50%. We're resolving 83% of all of our inquiries robotically. It's incredible. So, now, how do I get that message out? How do I do it globally? How do I find my KNMS moment where I can come up with something that's viral and exciting? (20:04): I'm trying lots of different things. I have Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson who are two friends of mine helping me. So they said, "We'll cut ads for you." They have not been together in an ad ever, and they haven't done anything together since True Detective. They're friends of mine. Again, very generous people to agree to do this. We've shot three ads so far. I put them out on Twitter to get feedback from folks. Is this a good idea? (20:35): I am running this help.salesforce.com to show what we can do with it. Is that a good idea? I'm training all my salespeople in how to sell it. Is that a good idea? I'm running aggressive marketing against Microsoft because they have really a terrible product, Copilot, that I have to position against and market against. Is that a good idea? Should I be marketing and positioning against them? (20:58): I'm trying lots of things, and what I'm trying to do, Lenny, is what I recommend to all entrepreneurs. The message is really in the medium here, which is that I am looking to try to find the winning tactic and turn it into a winning strategy. I don't know actually which one of those things is going to be the most important thing in launching this product, so I'm trying a lot of things with that old expression. I'm throwing everything against the wall. I'm looking at what's going to stick. Then, once I find that thing, I will then grow that as my strategy, and that is what I'm trying to do. (21:33): I'm even expanding my distribution organization. I'm trying to hire an additional one to 2,000 account executives just to focus on Agentforce. So I'm trying to do everything I can to get that light switch to go on where I can show customers this is an incredible opportunity to lower your cost, to make things better, and to show that for the first time, we can have digital labor, that Salesforce isn't just managing your data, but we're a digital labor provider. So this is that moment.
turns.zh: 嗯，Lenny，这真是个喧闹的世界，你也看得出来。你可以上推特看看。那里简直充斥着各种声音，如何才能脱颖而出？这正是我们今天面临的挑战。我们要推出一款名为Agentforce的重磅新产品。我开发这款产品才几个月。去年在Dreamforce大会上发布它，就是个突破口——我把整个大会专注于Agentforce。现在我正思考：要让公司、客户乃至所有人100%迁移到Agentforce，我还需要做哪些工作？因为我知道眼下是个绝佳机遇窗口。（19:25）：我们走在前列，遥遥领先。目前已有数百家客户在使用这款产品。我们的整个帮助中心都迁移到了Agentforce，效果惊人。人工干预请求减少了50%，83%的查询能通过机器人自动解决。太棒了。现在该如何扩大影响力？如何实现全球推广？如何抓住KNMS时刻，打造出病毒式传播的爆款？（20:04）：我尝试了多种方法。比如请来马修·麦康纳和伍迪·哈里森两位好友拍摄广告。他们自《真探》后就没再合作过，但这次欣然答应。已拍了三支广告，放到推特征求反馈。效果如何？（20:35）：我建了help.salesforce.com专页展示其功能。这样做对吗？我培训所有销售人员如何推广。这样做对吗？针对微软Copilot产品，我发起强势营销攻势。这样做对吗？我该不该专注于打压竞争对手？（20:58）：我尝试了各种方法，Lenny，这也是我给所有创业者的建议。关键在于策略落地——寻找制胜战术并将其转化为战略。我不确定哪项举措对产品推广最关键，所以采用了广撒网的策略。不断试错，找准突破口后再深化。这就是我的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much there that I love, this idea of trying a bunch of things, looking for the tactic that becomes your strategy. It feels like also there's this focus of just go all in and focus on this one thing, and then try a bunch of different ways for this one thing that you're focused on to win. There's also an element of... I just had Seth Godin on the podcast, and one of his big lessons is be remarkable. Create something people remark about. So this celeb-oriented ad that you're working on, I think, is a really good example of that.
turns.zh: 里面有太多我喜爱的内容——那种尝试各种方法，寻找能转化为战略的战术的理念。感觉还有一种专注于全力以赴、专注于手头这件事的思维模式，然后为你所专注的这件事尝试各种不同的获胜方式。还有一个要点……我最近在播客上采访了赛斯·高丁，他传授的一个重要经验就是要做到与众不同，创造出能让人们津津乐道的东西。所以你们正在做的这个以名人为核心的广告，我认为就是一个很好的例子。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Well, that is a key thought though that he's saying, which is you got to find it, but finding that is the hard part, so you got to be like... One of my friends is Chris Rock, the comedian. So what he'll do is he just doesn't go out and do a Netflix special with all of his jokes. He's out there testing his jokes in clubs and doing all kinds of crazy things. I won't go through all the crazy stuff he does to test his jokes, but by the time it gets to the big Netflix special, he knows what works and what doesn't work. So that is something that we all have to do as entrepreneurs. We need to be testing lots of things. We need a lot of experimentation, and we can't be too arrogant. (23:15): I think another thing that's extremely important is... I have a pretty deep meditation practice for three, four decades which is we have to be cultivating our beginner's mind. We have to use our mindfulness in a way to clear everything out and then get back to, "What is my beginner's mind?" In the beginner's mind, I have every possibility, but in the expert's mind, I have few, and in some cases, maybe none. So I've been doing this a long time. I've been writing software since I'm 15. I'm now 60. That's 45 years. I don't want to have an expert's mind. I want to have a beginner's mind, and how do I have that beginner's mind? Because those ideas will come at me if I can go, "What could work?" rather than saying, "Oh, I know what is going to work," or, "This is the one thing that is going to definitely work," or, "We have to do this." (24:10): As soon as you start using words like that, you know that you're going to completely implode and fail. You have to say, "Here, we have to do all these things." Like in my company right now, we just did this all-hands call. I was like, "There's six things I really want to get done," but one thing is I didn't get everybody focused on Agentforce and really watch the energy. Number two is I need to find more fuel in the company to fuel this idea because this is clearly a breakthrough product, so how do I get everyone focused on it? Number three, where I think it's really important, we need more distribution capability. We don't sell through franchises. We're not selling through dealers, resellers. We sell direct, so I know I need more account executives. (24:56): Number four is I need to be telling lots of customer stories. So, number one, customer zero, me, and number two is I need to tell you all the stories. Like, you can see the story of Disney. I'm doing a huge amount of AI work for them and Agentforce work. Let me tell you the story about Disney. I need to tell you that story, and then we have this whole ecosystem of people around the company called Trailblazers, millions of them, who know our platform. They all have to become agentblazers. (25:23): The last thing is I just shipped the product into all 135,000 Salesforce customers. So it's their nascent, and they need to flick it on. I need to motivate them to turn it on. These are the six things I'm thinking about all the time. So it's not just one thing. I'm trying to figure out what it is, and I need a beginner's mind to assess how do I move forward, how do I evolve, how do I inspire, how do I motivate, how do I energize.
turns.zh: 嗯，他说的是一个关键观点，就是你必须先找到方向，但找到方向是最难的部分。所以你得像……我的朋友克里斯·洛克（Chris Rock）那样。他不会直接去录制Netflix特别节目，把所有笑话都放进去。他会先在俱乐部里测试笑料，尝试各种疯狂的点子。我就不细说他测试笑料的那些疯狂举动了，但等到Netflix特别节目正式上线时，他已经知道哪些有效，哪些无效了。作为创业者，我们也必须这样做。我们需要不断测试各种想法，进行大量实验，不能太自负。（23:15）：我认为还有一点极其重要……我有三四十年的深度冥想修行，那就是我们必须培养初学者的心态。我们要用正念的方式清空思绪，然后问自己：“我的初学者心态是什么？” 在初学者的心态中，一切皆有可能；而在专家的心态中，可能性就很有限，甚至可能毫无可能。我这样做已经很久了。我从15岁就开始写软件，现在60岁了，有45年的经验。我不想拥有专家的心态，我想要保持初学者的心态。如何保持这种心态呢？因为当你能问“哪些方案可行？”而不是说“我知道什么能成功”或者“必须这样做”时，那些创意就会涌现出来。（24:10）：一旦你开始用这种语气说话，你就注定会彻底失败。必须要说：“现在，我们必须做这些事。” 比如，我公司最近开了一个全员会议。我想：“有六件事我特别想完成。” 但首先，我没能让大家专注于Agentforce，真正激发团队的能量。其次，我需要为这个产品找到更多燃料，因为这显然是一个突破性产品，那要怎么让大家都专注于它呢？第三，至关重要的是，我们需要更强的分销能力。我们不通过加盟店、经销商销售，而是直接销售，所以我知道需要更多客户经理。（24:56）：第四，我需要讲述大量客户案例。首先，客户零号就是我自己，其次要把所有案例都讲给你们听。比如，你们可以看看迪士尼的案例。我为他们和Agentforce做了大量AI工作。让我讲讲迪士尼的故事吧。我必须讲这个故事，然后我们公司还有一个叫Trailblazers的生态系统，数百万人使用我们的平台。他们都得成为Agentblazers。（25:23）：最后，我刚把产品推送给了所有135,000名Salesforce客户。所以现在他们才刚刚起步，需要把它启用起来。我得激励他们启用这些功能。以上就是我一直在思考的六件事。所以这不是单一的事情。我在努力弄清楚该怎么做，如何前进，如何进化，如何激励，如何动员，如何激发能量。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Well, Salesforce is now the second largest software company in the world, but also the second largest software company in Japan, and that's a country where I put a lot of time and energy into. I love going there. I love going to Kyoto. When I go to Kyoto, I like to go to some of these amazing Zen temples. By the way, that's one of the things that Steve Jobs love to do, and he used to go to these great sushi restaurants. There's a great one in Kyoto named Sushiiwa. If you go in there, you'll see he's signed something for them. It says, "All good things. Steve Jobs." I said, "What did he do over here?" He would go to this great sushi restaurant, and then he would go to Ryōan-ji, the Rock Garden Temple. Incredible metaphysical temple. (28:04): I've gone there. I've gone there for decades. I've brought a lot of friends of mine there. Yeah. You got to clear your mind and let it come in. You got to receive it. You need to listen. I remember I even brought Neil Young there, the musician. He's one of my favorite people in the world, and obviously, I love his music. His soundtrack is the soundtrack of my entire life. We were sitting there, and he was so deep in meditation, and then he started walking around. The temple was closing, and then he was in the zone, and I didn't want to bother him, but I'm like, "You know, I think we got to go." (28:38): Anyway, it turned out he had written a whole album while we were there in his head, and he was basically transcribing it all. This incredible creative process. Look, we're all writing an album in our head. What album are you writing? What music are you writing? How are you getting into that zone yourself? You want to be a great entrepreneur. You want to be a great CEO. You got to clear your mind, and you got to be ready to write that music. (29:06): That music could be your business plan, your product plan, your product launch plan like we're talking about for my Agentforce product. That's what we're all trying to do, and I use a place like Kyoto as a place to do that also because geography is important. Where you are matters. I know you're in Marin, so Marin County. Maybe you can go out to the top of Mount Tam. Maybe you go to Spirit Rock with Jack Kornfield and go clear your mind there, but you got to find the place to do that and create the location. It may not be in the office. It may be somewhere else.
turns.zh: 嗯，Salesforce现在是全球第二大软件公司，也是日本第二大软件公司，而日本是我投入大量时间和精力去探索的国家。我很喜欢去那里。我喜欢去京都。当我去京都时，我喜欢去那些令人惊叹的禅宗寺庙。顺便说一句，史蒂夫·乔布斯也喜欢做这件事，他常去那些很棒的寿司店。京都有一家叫Sushiiwa的寿司店。如果你去那里，你会看到他在那里签名了。上面写着：“一切美好。史蒂夫·乔布斯。” 我问：“他在这里做过什么？” 他会去这家很棒的寿司店，然后去龙安寺，那个岩石花园寺庙。真是令人惊叹的玄学寺庙。我去过那里。几十年来我一直去那里。我带过很多朋友去那里。是啊。你得清空思绪，让灵感涌现。你得接纳它。你需要倾听。我记得我甚至带尼尔·杨去过那里，这位音乐家。他是我在这个世界上最喜欢的人之一，很显然，我热爱他的音乐。他的配乐是我整个人生的配乐。我们坐在那里，他陷入了深深的冥想，然后开始四处走动。寺庙快关门了，而他正处于那种境界中，我不想打扰他，但我还是说了：“你知道的，我们得走了。” （28:04）：不管怎样，原来我们在那里的时候，他在脑海中构思了一整张专辑，基本上都是在把它全都记录下来。这是一个令人惊叹的创作过程。看，我们都在脑海中构思一张专辑。你在构思什么专辑呢？你在创作什么音乐呢？你自己又如何进入那种境界呢？你想成为一名伟大的企业家。你想成为一名伟大的CEO。你得清空思绪，准备好创作那段音乐。（29:06）：那段音乐可能是你的商业计划、产品计划、产品发布计划，就像我们现在谈论的Agentforce产品一样。这就是我们都在努力做的，而我把京都这样的地方也当作做这件事的地方，因为地理位置很重要。你在哪里很重要。我知道你在马林县，所以马林县。也许你可以去塔姆山山顶。也许你可以和杰克·科恩菲尔德一起去精神岩，清理思绪，但你得找到那个能让你做到这一点的地方，创造那个环境。它可能不在办公室里。它可能在其他地方。

The stock isn't the goal. It's coming at the end of the journey. It's like that's not why we're doing this. The journey is the reward. That's also something Steve Jobs would say all the time. Another bow to Steve Jobs here. I think that this is really important, and I look at myself as a startup. (31:05): I am a startup CEO. I'm a startup entrepreneur. I'm still at the beginning of Salesforce. No matter what I'm doing at Salesforce, whether I'm the CEO, I'm sometimes the chair of the board. Like, last week, we had a board meeting. Sometimes I'm a product manager. This is a startup, and we're a 25-year-old, 75,000-person, $38 billion, $300 something billion market cap startup, but we're a startup nonetheless. We have some great products, but we are just starting. As an example, Lenny, we are just starting the digital labor industry, and we have a product called Agentforce, and we are just starting. We are just at the beginning.
turns.zh: 我觉得关注股票走势会让人分心，我也鼓励我的员工不要过度关注股票，因为股价只是一种反映。钱不是最终目标，对吧？股票不是终点，而是旅程的终点。这不是我们做事的初衷。旅程本身才是最大的回报。史蒂夫·乔布斯也常这么说。我认为这很重要，我把自己视为一家初创公司的创始人。（31:05）我是一位初创公司的CEO，一位创业者。Salesforce仍处在发展初期。无论我在Salesforce担任何种角色——CEO、董事会主席（上周刚开完董事会），还是产品经理——这始终是一家初创公司。我们是一家拥有25年历史、7.5万名员工、市值380亿美元的初创企业，但本质上我们依然是初创公司。我们拥有优秀的产品，但才刚刚起步。举个例子，伦尼，我们刚刚涉足数字劳动力行业，推出了名为Agentforce的产品，这才刚刚开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to bounce around a little bit, but let's talk about Agentforce. I know this is, as you've said, the thing you're most focused on right now. It's a big bet you all are taking. When people hear this word "agent," I think a lot of people are embarrassed to even ask like, "What does that even look like? What is an agent beyond what LLMs are today?" Is there an example you could give of something you've seen that maybe blew your mind of what an agent can do?
turns.zh: 我想再深入探讨一下Agentforce。我知道正如你所说，这是你目前最关注的项目。这是大家下的大赌注。当人们听到“智能客服”这个词时，我觉得很多人都不好意思问：“这到底是个什么概念？除了当下LLM技术的应用外，智能客服还能做些什么？” 你能否举个例子，展示智能客服的强大功能，让我们大开眼界？

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Yeah. I saw it in the movies. I saw it in Minority Report, which was a movie that was co-written by our futurist, Peter Schwartz. Tom Cruise runs into the Gap store, and all of a sudden, it says, "Hey. Hey, Tom. Have you thought about this new shirt? Look at these jeans. You bought this last time. Now, you could try this. You could try that. What about this? What about that?" It knew his history. It understood him. It knew what was going on. This is 20 years ago. This whole store changes digitally to reflect his interest, his ideas, and it's starting to talk to him and work with him. (32:51): That is an agent. It isn't just the agent that we saw in the Matrix, Mr. Smith, or whatever it is. It's someone that's working with you, someone. That's an interesting, for you, slip. It's something that is working with you. It could be your piece of software in your phone. It could be a robot that's going to be in your home. It could be your car that knows you, understands your preferences, has an institutional memory of you, and now is helping to advise you. (33:22): I'll give you an example that I'm going to... I go into UCSF all the time. I'm actually just getting through an Achilles rupture right now, so I've had a lot of interactions, and the hospital... or you're getting your healthcare, getting your labs done, getting your physical done, getting your scans done, whatever it is. There's always these pre-operative and post-operative or pre-procedure and post-procedure things, and you're getting these phone calls. Every time I get a phone call, I'm like, "Ugh, that probably just cost them a hundred bucks, and we probably could do that a lot cheaper and a lot easier with an agent." (33:58): Then, when I talk to my doctors and nurses at UCSF, they're all burnt out post-pandemic because they're scheduling pajama time to go through all their digital messages at night. It's like a lot of this could be done a lot easier with agents and AI, and we're going to make their lives a lot better, a lot easier, simpler. Some of those things that they're doing, they don't need to talk to me about what my cholesterol number is because I got my labs, and the cholesterol number is this number or that number. A lot of this can be done with technology, and then save the parts that are important for them like when I come to see them or I want to have a real, deeper, more empathetic conversation face-to-face with a deeply experienced doctor. That's a whole another opportunity for me. (34:45): That is an agent or the agent is like... Here's an example. I had a CT scan, and you have to drink this contrast, and then all of a sudden, the... drink it, but they give it to you through an IV, and then they're taking better pictures. But then, you have to drink water to flush the contrast out of your body. Do you think anyone called me and said, "Hey, did you drink the water?" No, nobody calls me to drink the water. You have to remember. You're on your own in healthcare in the US. So the agent is going to call you and say, "Hey, did you drink the water? Did you take your meds? Do you need to have a repeat lab? Do you need to go see your doctor again?" So the agent is going to be there by your side. So that's an healthcare example. There's a lot of examples that we can probably have.
turns.zh: 是啊。我在电影里见过这种场景。比如《少数派报告》，这部电影是由我们的未来学家彼得·施瓦茨参与编剧的。汤姆·克鲁斯冲进盖璞（Gap）商店，突然屏幕上跳出提示：“嘿，汤姆。你有没有注意到这件新衬衫？看看这条牛仔裤，上次你买的就是这个。现在你可以试试这件，再看看那件怎么样？”系统能读懂他的购物历史，精准理解他的需求。（32:51）：这就是智能代理。它不只是《黑客帝国》里史密斯先生那样的虚拟助手，而是真正与你互动的存在。比如你的手机软件、家中机器人或者懂你喜好的汽车，都能成为你的智能伙伴。（33:22）：我举个例子。我常去加州大学旧金山分校（UCSF），目前刚经历了跟腱断裂手术，跟医院打交道很多。无论是预约检查、做实验室检查、看扫描结果，还是术前术后护理，总有各种繁琐的流程和重复的电话提醒。每次接到电话我都烦躁不已：“天啊，这得花他们一百美元啊！用智能代理不就能省下这笔钱吗？”（33:58）：再说和UCSF的医生护士沟通，他们因为疫情后士气低落，晚上还要挤时间处理堆积如山的信息。很多重复工作本可以用智能代理自动化，让他们的生活更轻松。比如检查胆固醇值时，护士会打电话告知结果，但其实我自己就能查到数据。智能助手能处理大量琐碎事务，把精力留给真正需要面对面交流的深层医护场景。这对我来说是全新的机遇。（34:45）：智能代理还能像这样：做完CT扫描后要喝造影剂，他们通过静脉注射给你药液，扫描效果更好。但最后你得自己喝水排出造影剂。有人会打电话提醒你吗？没有啊。你得自己操心。美国医疗体系就是这样。所以智能代理会主动问：“你喝水了吗？吃药了吗？需要复查化验吗？要再去看医生吗？”它会全程陪伴你。这就是医疗场景中的智能代理。类似的应用场景还有很多。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Yeah. turns.zh: 是的。他们做了一项临床研究，通过半同行评审的方式发现，ChatGPT在很多情况下给出的诊断比医生更准确，因为医生在与患者合作时存在更大的主观偏见。这真的很引人深思，我认为我们都应该仔细研究这项研究并加以思考。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Well, I keep having these existential freakout moments about AI, and it's happened over a series of decades. But for those of us who grew up with these movies like WarGames and Minority Report or Her or... across the board or read some of these books. One of my favorite books on AI is Ghost Fleet. You think about, "Where are we going with AI? Where are we going with AI?" With Salesforce, I think about our journey, and I've been waiting for this to happen and trying to bring us along, especially in the last decade with the development of our Einstein platform, and now the development of our Agentforce platform. (37:18): This week, at Salesforce, we'll probably do about 2 trillion AI transactions. With our total now, Einstein and Agentforce platforms, we're definitely the largest provider of enterprise AI transactions in the world as far as I could tell, and I keep thinking, "Wow, this is going to get more and more intense." One step was we had to automate all these customer touch points. So like wearing my Disney fanboy shirt here, we run the Disney Store and the Disney Guides, and there's Disney Real Estate, and there's the DisneyQuest call center, and there's... Every aspect of Disney. When you're a customer, you're interfacing with Salesforce. (38:00): So that's what we've loved doing, automating all these customer touch points: sales, service, marketing, analytics, Slack, integrating it all with MuleSoft. That's what we do, and then aggregating it all into a big database where we call it data cloud, and then federating that data cloud to other data sources. So that's the two steps we've been doing, automate the customer touch points, aggregate the data, and then step three is the agentic platform on top of that. (38:29): When you think about what's happening now that you can go to help.salesforce.com and have your issues resolved with that on the agentic layer, that's amazing. Then, the fourth layer that will come will be the robotic drone layer where those robots and drones will then feed off of the platform and all of these capabilities. That vision of the future is something that we've all had in the industry for years. It's not my magic vision. This is a vision that's been around. It's been the fundamentals of computer science that we would move from having... We'd go from data to automation, and that is what we're all driving, and we're driving that industry. We're going lower cost, easier to use, and more automated constantly. That's powerful. This is really moving fast.
turns.zh: 嗯，我对人工智能一直有种存在主义的恐慌感，这种情绪已经持续了几十年。但对于我们这些看着《战争游戏》《少数派报告》《她》等电影长大的人，或者读过相关书籍的人来说（比如我最喜欢的关于人工智能的书《幽灵舰队》），你会不禁思考：“我们要把人工智能带向何方？”在Salesforce，我一直在思考我们的发展历程。过去十年间，我们致力于开发Einstein平台和Agentforce平台，一直在推动行业进步。（37:18）本周，Salesforce可能将处理约2万亿次人工智能交易。凭借Einstein和Agentforce平台，我们无疑已成为全球最大的企业级人工智能交易提供商。我总在想：“这股浪潮只会愈演愈烈。”第一步是自动化所有客户接触点。比如，我们负责迪士尼商店和迪士尼指南服务，还有迪士尼房地产和迪士尼Quest呼叫中心等迪士尼业务的各个环节。作为客户，你在每个迪士尼触点都会接触到Salesforce。（38:00）自动化所有客户接触点是我们热爱做的事：销售、服务、营销、分析、Slack，以及通过MuleSoft将所有系统整合。接下来是数据聚合，第三步是构建智能平台。（38:29）现在你可以访问help.salesforce.com，通过智能平台层解决问题，这真是太棒了。未来还将推出机器人无人机层，所有机器人和无人机都将接入这个平台，共享这些能力。这种未来愿景在业界已酝酿多年。这并非我的独创，而是计算机科学的基本发展路径——从数据到自动化，这正是我们整个行业的驱动力，不断降低成本、提升易用性和自动化程度。这力量实在强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny

I know you've said you're not going to be hiring as many engineers next year. I guess anything there to help people understand how the workforce will change in the future?
turns.zh: 太可爱了。当你谈论这一切时，我想很多人会想，"哦，该死，我们的工作机会会减少。我们该怎么办呢？AI作为代理人。"我知道你说的任何话都可能被断章取义，人们会说"马克·贝尼奥夫说每个人都失业了"，但我想只是...我知道你说过明年不会招聘那么多工程师。我猜有没有什么能帮助人们理解未来劳动力将如何变化的信息？

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Well, I can tell you about my own company and what I'm telling my own employees, which is that, yeah, we're going to have to rebalance some of our workforce because you can see it in the numbers I just gave you which is we need less support engineers because we have a robotic support layer with Agentforce. So that is very real, and we all need to adapt. At the same time, I'm hiring a lot more account executives and folks to grow the company. So I just encouraged everybody on the all-hands call to think about that. (41:06): Then, I just gave you the idea of healthcare. The interesting thing about healthcare though is that a lot of the jobs that I think that are going to get created just... we don't have people for, and I think there's a lot of things that we need help with in the world that we don't have people for. So I think a lot of these jobs will not necessarily get replaced, and I think that... I have a home in a small town, and in this small town... It's very much a blue-collar town. Folks are still working in the restaurants, driving trucks, working in the supermarket, and working on their homes, building, construction, gardening. (41:56): Look, it's going to be a long time before, I think, jobs in the small town where I have a home will ever get impacted. But in the large town where I have a home, San Francisco, well, then I just gave you an example where I think that jobs will get impacted. So it'll be a tale of two cities, literally, and I think you will see different impacts in different places.
turns.zh: 嗯，我可以谈谈我自己的公司，以及我对员工说的话，那就是，是的，我们确实需要重新平衡一部分劳动力，因为你可以从我刚刚给出的数字中看到，我们需要更少的支持工程师，因为我们有Agentforce的机器人支持层。所以这很真实，我们都需要适应。与此同时，我正在招聘更多的客户执行和公司发展人员。所以我在全员大会上鼓励每个人都考虑这一点。（41:06）：然后，我刚刚给了你一个医疗保健的例子。不过医疗保健领域有趣的是，我认为将要创造的许多工作岗位...我们找不到合适的人选。我认为世界上有很多我们需要帮助的事情，但我们找不到合适的人选。所以我认为许多这些工作岗位不一定会被取代，我在一个小镇有房子，小镇...这是一个蓝领小镇。人们仍然在餐馆工作，开卡车，在超市工作，修缮房子，搞建筑，种花。（41:56）：看，我认为在我家乡的小镇，工作机会被影响还需要很长时间。但在我家乡的大城市旧金山，嗯，我刚刚给了一个例子，我认为那里的工作机会会受到影响。所以这将是两个城市的故事，字面意义上的，我想你会看到不同地方有不同的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing there is support people trending down, account executive sales trending up?
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是支持人员数量在减少，客户执行和销售人员数量在增加？

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Right now, that is Salesforce in a nutshell.
turns.zh: 目前，这就是Salesforce的概况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That touches on something I wanted to touch on also which is that you're... A lot of founders today are very product-minded, very product-oriented founders, and they want to build product-first companies, grow product-led, all these things. Salesforce, I think, very publicly, is very sales-led, very marketing-led, not product-led. Obviously, product is a core part of it, and it all works together, and all these things. But I guess just any advice for founders that are very product-oriented and maybe are hesitant to lean into sales, into cust-
turns.zh: 这也涉及到我想要谈到的另一个问题，那就是你们...如今很多创始人非常以产品为导向，非常以产品为导向的创始人，他们想建立以产品为先的公司，发展以产品为主导的业务，诸如此类。但我认为Salesforce公开来说非常以销售为导向，非常以营销为导向，而不是以产品为导向。显然，产品是其核心部分，一切都协同运作，但我猜对于那些非常以产品为导向、可能不愿重视销售、重视客户服务的创始人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Yeah. I would say we're not sales-led. Well, I think let's just use Agentforce as an example, right?
turns.zh: 是的。我得说我们不是以销售为导向的。嗯，我想就拿Agentforce来举例吧，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: So we're running the year, we're running this year. This is our fiscal year 25. Okay? It ends in the end of January next year. Lenny, this is the year of data cloud. This was not supposed to be the year of Agentforce. So it's the year of data cloud. I just gave you the pitch. We've automated all the customer touch points. Now, we're adding the data cloud to all of our customer implementations. We have 135,000 customers. We've implemented data cloud into all of them. They all need to turn it on. Our teams need to show our customers how to build data cloud and how it's going to help our customers have a better data structure. I almost combined "beta" and "data" together. So they need a better data structure, data architectures, data cultures. (43:51): Then, we had our breakthrough, and I can tell you the story where all of a sudden, I'm like, "Wow, this agent technology is happening much faster than I thought it was going to, and we are going to market now." By the time we get to Dreamforce, we are going to take this incredible technology. We accelerated it radically because we bought this company called Airkit, which is one of our Ohana... It's a great story. (44:18): Great entrepreneur have this company, fantastic company called RelateIQ that we bought many years ago, about 10 years ago, stayed with us for many years, like six or seven years, wanted to leave, and we said, "Great." We gave them the investment to leave, invested in the company through Salesforce Ventures, built this amazing platform, and then we said, "Now, we want to buy it back." Then, he came back about a year ago, and then it just accelerated the agent vision, and then we delivered Agentforce production code at the end of October. So, all of a sudden, now, we are releasing this product. (44:56): I think it's very important, if you're an entrepreneur, to realize it's not just about the product. It's not just about sales. It's not just about marketing. It's not just about accounting. It's not just about your investors. It's not just about your employees. It's not just about your stakeholders. It's about everything, so you better be ready to be an orchestra leader. You can't just be playing the clarinet. (45:20): I think that's what you're getting to, which is that there's entrepreneurs who are like, "I'm just going to play the clarinet." For those, I don't think they're going to go as far as they could go. You want to be playing the whole symphony, and you want to get everyone running. That symphony is sales, service, marketing, product. Every part of your shareholders, your stakeholders, your customers. You have to be constantly playing the whole symphony, and you have to have a big mind to think about, "Whoa, I have a lot of stakeholders in my company, not just one stakeholder." It's not just about product and technology. If you're going to narrowcast yourself, you're doing a disservice not just to yourself, but to everybody else as well.
turns.zh: 所以我们正在度过这个财年，也就是我们当前的25财年。好吗？它将于明年1月底结束。莱尼，今年是数据云之年。本来说今年不该是Agentforce之年。所以今年是数据云之年。我刚给你们介绍了我们的战略。我们已经把所有客户接触点都实现了自动化。现在，我们要把数据云功能整合到所有客户的实施项目中。我们有13.5万个客户，所有客户都已经接入了数据云。他们都需要启用这项功能。我们的团队需要向客户展示如何构建数据云，以及它将如何帮助客户优化数据架构。（43:51）：然后，我们迎来了突破时刻。我可以跟你们讲讲那个故事——突然间，我意识到‘哇，代理技术的发展速度比我预期的快得多，我们现在就要推向市场了。’等我们参加Dreamforce大会时，我们将推出这项令人惊叹的技术。由于收购了Airkit公司（我们的Ohana成员之一），我们得以极大地加速其发展……这是一个很棒的故事。（44:18）：我们收购了RelateIQ公司（一家很棒的初创企业，收购于约10年前，合作了六七年，他们本想离开，但我们说‘没关系’。我们通过Salesforce Ventures投资支持他们，打造了这个出色的平台，然后又说‘现在我们要把它买回来’。大约一年前，他们回归了，这极大地推动了代理技术的进程，最终我们在10月底交付了Agentforce的生产代码。所以，突然间，我们就要发布这款产品了。（44:56）：我认为，如果你是一位创业者，就必须意识到成功不只是关乎产品、销售、市场营销、会计或投资者，也不只是关乎员工或利益相关者，而是关乎方方面面。因此，你最好要具备管弦乐队指挥的才能，不能只演奏单一乐器。（45:20）：我觉得这正是你们所要表达的——有些创业者只想‘演奏单一乐器’。对于这类人，我认为他们无法充分发挥潜力。你需要指挥整个交响乐，推动所有部门运作。这部交响乐包括销售、服务、市场营销和产品开发，涵盖股东、利益相关者和客户等所有方方面面。你必须持续演奏这部交响乐，还要有宏观视野，意识到‘哇，我们公司有众多利益相关者，而不只是单一股东。’成功不只是关乎产品和技术。如果你只关注狭隘领域，不仅对自己不利，也会对他人造成伤害。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of big mind and beginner's mind, we have a recurring segment on this podcast that I call Fail Corner. Where it comes from is people come on this podcast, they share all these stories of, "Everything is going great. We're killing it. I've had all these successes," and people get discouraged because they hear just people only succeeding when they often fail. So I try to ask guests to share a story, and let me ask you this. Is there a story you could share when it was a big struggle for you when you're struggling when something went super wrong that you worked through and learned something from?
turns.zh: 说到“大格局思维”和“初学者心态”，我们播客里有个固定环节，我称之为“失败角”。这个环节的灵感来源于这样一种现象：嘉宾们来做客播客时，总会分享各种成功故事——“一切进展顺利，我们势头正猛，我取得了诸多成就”之类的。但听众们往往会感到沮丧，因为他们听来都是那些在经历多次失败后才成功的人的故事。所以我会邀请嘉宾们分享一个故事，我想问问你们，有没有过这样一段经历：当事情进展得一团糟时，你如何挺过难关，从中汲取教训？

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Sure. Well, I'll just give this example. About two years ago, we went through this huge transformation in our company, and there were a lot of crazy things that were happening, but it was a little bit like we're all on this Airplane, and everything is going really well. Then, something seems to be going really wrong, and we look up front, and the two pilots seemed to be missing. Then, the one guy with the parachute jumped out of the plane, and then we're all like, "Whoa, what are we going to do?" We had to do some really crazy and somewhat destructive things at the moment to basically get the regeneration of the company. (47:12): One of those things that we did two years ago was we had to architect a layoff, and we had never done a scaled layoff before. We had to lay off 10% of the company to save the company, and I didn't want to do it. I mean, it's the last thing I want to do as an entrepreneur, which is to adjust our headcount, but we were coming out of the pandemic, and we had just hired too many people. (47:33): Now, it turned out that a lot of companies in Silicon Valley all did that same maneuver during the pandemic. Things were so robust in the pandemic that we were overhiring. By the time the pandemic was over, we had too many people. I mean, what did I know? It was my first pandemic. All of a sudden, my next pandemic, I'll know that there's an economic cycle associated with it and an inflation cycle too. (47:58): So I learned a lot in the pandemic, and now, we're here. Now, all of a sudden, we're architecting two years ago this layoff. Then, when we did the layoff, then I'm trying to overcommunicate. I'm having all employee meetings. It's a complete dumpster fire. It's a nightmare. I'm getting bashed in the press, on Twitter. Everyone is shooting at me. It's like, "Oh, boy." If I had a thick skin, it got a lot thicker during that moment because it's never going to go well no matter what, and it didn't go well but we got through it to the point where you're giving me these accolades, wonderful, on this podcast about where we are today financially and from a structural standpoint or now from product innovation standpoint, but that's not where we were two years ago. (48:51): It was clear we had to go through a financial transformation, which included an adjustment of our head count, and we had to go through a technology, and a product, and an innovation transformation. Those two things were going to require us to do a number of things, and they were going to be painful. So we all had to go through some of that pain to get the gain that we have now, and that was not easy. (49:17): I was in shock that I was going through this two years ago because I had already been running the company for 23 years. Things were going pretty well. Yes, there were a lot of failures during that period. I just didn't expect another massive issue to hit me. But guess what? There're constantly massive issues coming at you, and there's more coming, and that's the nature. (49:39): My friend, Michael Bell, is probably the best entrepreneur I know. He says, "There is no linear success." So what that means is that stock chart that you just referred to, there's no up-and-to-the-right perfect chart where it's just one line. I don't care who you are. Apple doesn't have one. No one has one. Okay? There's going to be changes. It could be economic changes. It could be societal changes. It could be the pandemic. There's no up-and-to-the-right. If you think it's only going to be about up and to the right, you're in the wrong business or you have the wrong life. Right? Hey, the monastic life is maybe more for you where you're just out living in that more of that steady state. Right? But if you want more variation where it's not steady state, the entrepreneurial life is a rock-and-roll roller coaster, and you get ready because it's going to be pounding you all the time.
turns.zh:
好的。嗯，我来举个例子。大约两年前，我们公司经历了一次重大变革，当时有很多疯狂的事情在发生，但就像我们都坐在一架飞机上，起初一切进展顺利。然后突然出现重大问题，我们抬头一看，发现两位飞行员不见了。接着，有个戴着降落伞的人跳出了飞机，我们所有人都惊呼：“天哪，我们该怎么办？”为了让公司重生，我们当时不得不采取一些极端且具有破坏性的措施。  

（47:12）：两年前我们做的一件事是策划裁员行动，而我们从未进行过大规模裁员。为了拯救公司，我们裁掉了10%的员工。我当时并不想这么做，作为创业者，我最不愿做的事就是调整团队规模。但当时正值疫情过后，我们招募了过多员工。回想起来，谁能想到呢？那是我经历的第一场疫情。突然间，下一次疫情来临时，我才意识到经济周期和通胀周期是相互关联的。  

（47:58）：所以我在疫情中吸取了教训，如今我们站在新起点。两年前策划的裁员行动再次浮上心头。实施裁员时，我竭尽全力沟通，召开员工大会，整个过程简直一团糟。媒体和推特上铺天盖地批评，所有人都在攻击我。那种感觉真是糟糕透顶。如果说我以前脸皮薄，那这次事件让我变得更厚了。因为无论如何事情都不会一帆风顺，虽然结果不尽如人意，但我们最终挺了过来，现在你们能看到我们在财报、架构或产品创新方面的亮眼表现，但两年前可不是这样。  

（48:51）：很明显，我们必须经历财务转型，包括调整人员规模，以及技术、产品和创新方面的变革。这些变革注定充满痛苦。但为了换取今天的成果，我们必须承受这些痛苦，确实很不易。  

（49:17）：两年前经历这些时，我震惊不已，毕竟我已经经营公司23年了。一切原本进展顺利。是的，那段时期也经历了诸多失败，但我从未预料到会遭遇如此严重的危机。可猜猜怎么着？危机永远接踵而至，而且还会更多，这就是商业的本质。  

（49:39）：我的朋友迈克尔·贝尔是我认识的最优秀的企业家。他说：“成功没有线性轨迹。”这意味着你提到的股票图表，不可能是一条笔直上升的完美曲线，没有人能做到。苹果公司也做不到。任何公司都做不到。明白吗？变化是必然的。可能是经济环境的变动，也可能是社会结构的调整，甚至是疫情的冲击。没有笔直上升的轨迹。如果你以为成功只会是一帆风顺，那你选错了行业，或者过错的不是别人，就是你自己。
是吧？嘿，修道生活或许更适合你，你可以过上那种更稳定、安定的生活。没错吧？但如果你渴望更多变化，渴望那种非稳定状态的生活，那么创业生涯就像过山车般跌宕起伏，你得做好准备，因为它会时刻给你带来挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of these people that you described that jumped out of the airplane speaking on the roller coaster ride is your co-CEO, Bret Taylor. What's interesting to me is he's also all-in on agents, and what it makes me think about is there's this meme of what did Ilya see when he left and tried to kick out Sam Altman. I'm curious just like what did you guys see about agents being the future that you're both so committed to this? So interesting.
turns.zh: 你提到的那个从飞机上跳下来、在过山车上发言的人，是你的联席首席执行官布雷特·泰勒。让我感兴趣的是，他对代理商也全力投入。这让我联想到网上那个梗：伊利亚离开公司后试图赶走山姆·奥尔特曼时看到了什么？我很好奇，你们俩为什么都如此坚信代理商是未来的趋势？这真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: Well, I just think that this idea that agents are one of the most important things that we're all going to work on, and I think everyone is going to go to agents. Look, I just heard about Google today has Agentspace. At first, I was like, "Well, I guess they like the Agentforce name." I love Sundar. He's one of my favorite people in the world. We heard Microsoft now has agents. I read Oracle has agents now. SAP has agents. Everybody's got agents, and good. That's what we want. We don't want to be the only one. (51:30): If you're the only one and no one else is working on it, you've got a problem, actually. So you don't want to be the only one. You want to be in a market. You don't want to be one company offering a solution and the only one. You want to be in a competitive market where people are competing with you, and you're selling against somebody else, and you're getting better, and you're moving forward. It's like the automobile industry. One of my favorite people is Akio Toyoda. Toyoda-san was now the Chairman of Toyota, was the CEO of Toyota. His grandfather started Toyota. He says, "Better, better, better. Never best." It's the Japanese motto of Kaizen. (52:10): So we talked about Japanese Shoshin, which means beginner's mind. Now, we're learning another Japanese word here, Kaizen. Kaizen is continuous improvement, and you need to be doing continuous improvement. With where we are right now with agents, every software industry is going to move to agents. We have to just like every software industry... Well, at least in CRM or automating customer touchpoints, data and managing data, and building that data infrastructure, agents. It's all related. We're all moving in the same direction.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为代理商是我们所有人都需要全力投入的重要领域，而且我相信每个人最终都会转向代理商模式。比如今天我听说谷歌推出了Agentspace。起初我还想，"他们可能用了Agentforce这个名字吧。"我很喜欢孙达尔（Sundar Pichai），他是我最崇拜的人之一。我们听说微软现在也有代理商功能了。我读到甲骨文也加入了代理商阵营。SAP也加入了进来。这太棒了，这正是我们希望看到的。我们不想成为唯一一家在做这件事的公司。（51:30）如果你孤军奋战，没有其他人跟进，那才是问题所在。所以你不希望成为唯一一家。市场应该竞争激烈，人们相互竞争，你才能不断提升，持续前进。这就像汽车行业。我最欣赏的人之一是丰田章男。丰田章男现在是丰田的董事长兼CEO，他的祖父创立了丰田。他说：“更好，更好，更好。永远不追求完美。”这就是日本精益改善的理念。（52:10）我们之前讨论过日本的“初心”，意思是保持初学者的心态。现在我们又学习了另一个日本词汇——“精益改善”。精益改善意味着持续改进，而我们现在正朝着这个方向努力。代理商模式将席卷整个软件行业。每个软件行业都将向代理商转型。我们必须像其他行业一样——至少在客户关系管理、自动化客户接触点、数据管理和数据基础设施方面——全力投入代理商技术。这些领域息息相关，我们都在朝着同一个方向前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm just thinking as a founder, you're just like, "Goddamn, I just got used to AI, and everyone is wanting to work on AI in my company. Now, we got to freaking figure out agents?"
turns.zh: 作为创始人，我当时就想：“天啊，我才刚适应人工智能，结果公司里每个人都想做人工智能。现在我们又要操心代理商了？”

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: No, no, no, no, no. That's a mistake. That is the mindset you want. You want that mindset. You want the mindset of, "Oh, the next thing is coming. I can't wait for the next thing." In some ways, you have to be saying, "I can't wait for the next failure. I can't wait for the next success. I can't wait for the next innovation." Oh, well, that's innovation overall, right? (53:18): See, we're in an industry where technology is constantly getting lower cost, easier to use, and more automated. So if you're doing for two and a half decades, or four decades, or four and a half decades now that I've been doing it... When I started in this industry, I started on a computer called the TRS-80 Model I with 4K of RAM. I was doing a podcast recently, and they're like, "Well, who did you sell your first piece of software to?" I said, "Well, I sold it to CLOAD Magazine in Goleta, California and-
turns.zh: 不，不，不，不。这才是我们需要的思维模式。你要保持这种心态。就像“哦，下一个热点来了，我迫不及待想尝试。”从某种角度看，你必须不断告诉自己：“我等不及迎接下一次失败了。我等不及迎接下一次成功了。我等不及迎接下一次创新了。” 哦，这就是创新的本质，对吧？（53:18）你看，我们所处的行业，技术成本不断降低，使用门槛越来越低，自动化程度也越来越高。如果你在这个行业深耕了25年、40年，甚至像我一样已经做了四年半……我刚入行时，用的还是4K内存的TRS-80 Model I电脑。最近我在播客上被问：“你第一款软件卖给了谁？”我说：“哦，我卖给了加州戈莱塔的CLOAD杂志……”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For $75.
turns.zh: 只卖了75美元。

turns.speaker: Marc Benioff
turns.en: For $75, and they said, "Thank you for..." and then they said, "Oh, that's great, and did you send them the disk?" I'm like, "No, no. There was no disk. CLOAD standard for Cassette Load in BASIC. That was the command in BASIC, C-L-O-A-D, Cassette Load, CLOAD. That was the command. So that was the name of their magazine, and then you would get the cassette every month with five or six things that they had bought from people like me." I mean, they didn't know they were buying it from a 15-year-old kid in high school in Burlingame High School California. But I had written the How to Juggle thing, and they bought it for $75. They sent me the one-page agreement, and I signed it. Then, I told my parents, and they're like, "What? Huh? You're doing what? Oh, okay. That's nice, honey. Great job." (54:45): So they didn't understand. Nobody knew. It was crazy. It was like 1979 or 1978, so nobody knew I was selling software. I was in high school. It was just a moment in time, but I need to have that mindset all the way along which is, "What is the next great thing? What is the next great success? What is the next great failure?" You're growing. You're evolving. You're learning from that. That's what you want. You want to have that growth mindset. Right? You want to embrace that. Does it make sense what I said?
turns.zh: 花75美元，他们说：“谢谢你……”，然后又说：“哦，太棒了。你给他们寄磁盘了吗？”我说：“不，不。没有磁盘。CLOAD是BASIC语言中的磁带加载命令。就是这个命令。CLOAD。就是这个名字。每个月你都会收到磁带，里面有五六个从像我这样的人那里购买的内容。”我是说，那些人不知道他们买的是来自加利福尼亚州伯灵格姆高中15岁高中的孩子的东西。但我写了《如何玩杂耍》的文章，他们花75美元买了下来。他们给我寄了一页协议，我签了字。然后，我告诉父母，他们说：“什么？哈？你在做什么？哦，好吧。不错，亲爱的。干得好。”（54:45）：所以他们不明白。没人知道。这太疯狂了。那是1979年或1978年，所以没人知道我在卖软件。我还在上高中。那只是一段时光，但我需要一直保持这种心态：“下一个伟大的事情是什么？下一个巨大的成功是什么？下一个巨大的失败又是什么？” 你一直在成长。你在不断进步。你从中吸取教训。这才是你想要的。你需要有这种成长型思维。是吧？你需要欣然接受。这说得通吗？

turns.en: I jumped on that one little thought. "Oh, gee, yeah. I've got this now under control, but now I've got agents, so now, what am I going to..." It's like, "No, that's what you want." turns.zh: 我抓住了那个小想法。“哦，天哪，是啊。我现在已经控制住局面了，但现在我有代理商了，所以现在，我要……” 但不，这才是你想要的。顺便说一句，我也想知道接下来会发生什么，再下一个，再下一个。这才是未来最令人兴奋的地方。它即将到来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: I want to be... One of our customers said this, and people think I said it. It wasn't me. I want to get to the future first and welcome our customers there. That's what I think is... turns.zh: 我想成为……我们的一个客户说过这话，但人们以为是我说的。不是我。我想先到达未来，然后欢迎我们的客户到来。对我来说，这才是……顺便说一句，这也是我认为埃隆·马斯克做得非常好的地方。他就像……我不知道他为了预见未来做了多少疯狂的事情。他显然在做一些不同寻常的事情，但然后他会说：“是的，未来我们会有机器人，脑机接口，开电动车。所有这些事情都会在未来发生，而我将拥有10家公司来实现所有这些目标。” 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's not only thinking about it, he's doing them each.

turns.en: Amazing,
